themes.label: Introduction: Markov switching vs. linear nonstationarity models
themes.need: Someone modeling a nonstationary macro series (e.g. GNP) needs the case for a discrete-state Markov-switching alternative to linear ARIMA/unobserved-components/cointegration approaches, situating it relative to Goldfeld-Quandt switching regression, Kalman-filter analogies, and the paper's own filter/smoother contribution.

themes.label: Markov trend definition and transition probabilities
themes.need: Someone specifying a trend subject to discrete regime shifts needs the Markov-trend-in-levels definition (eq. 2.1), the two-state first-order Markov transition probabilities (eq. 2.2), and the AR(1) representation of the state process (eq. 2.3-2.4) with its non-Gaussian innovation distribution.

themes.label: Conditional and unconditional state probabilities
themes.need: Someone wanting the probability that the system is in a given regime at a future date, conditional on current information, needs the conditional-probability recursion and its closed form (eq. 2.5-2.9) in terms of the ergodic (unconditional) state probability.

themes.label: Noise-added model and its MA(1) representation
themes.need: Someone comparing the Markov trend to a standard linear ARIMA model needs the noise-added specification and its equivalent MA(1) representation (eq. 2.8-2.13), highlighting how it differs from a Gaussian AR(1)/MA(1) despite sharing the same autocovariance structure.

themes.label: Forecasting a Markov trend in levels and present-value calculations
themes.need: Someone wanting to forecast the future level, not just growth rate, of a series with a Markov trend, or compute a present value of its future cash flows, needs the levels-forecasting formulas and present-value results (eq. 3.1-3.5) for the Markov-trend-in-levels case.

themes.label: Markov trend in logs: forecast recursion setup
themes.need: Someone wanting to forecast a series whose log follows a Markov trend (the empirically relevant GNP case) needs the recursive setup (eq. 3.6-3.14) needed to derive its optimal forecast and present-value formulas, given the nonlinear (multiplicative) nature of the log-trend.

themes.label: Expected value and present-value results for the log Markov trend
themes.need: Someone wanting closed-form forecast and present-value expressions for a Markov trend in logs needs the final expected-value and present-value results (eq. 3.15-3.17) derived from the recursion, showing how they nest the levels case.

themes.label: Stochastic specification: Markov trend plus ARIMA noise
themes.need: Someone wanting to fit the Markov-trend model to actual data needs the full stochastic specification combining a Markov trend with an ARIMA noise component (eq. 4.1-4.3), the working example used for the rest of the estimation sections.

themes.label: The basic recursive filter
themes.need: Someone wanting to draw probabilistic inference about the unobserved regime from observed data needs the five-step recursive filtering algorithm that updates the state probability each period given the new observation.

themes.label: Filter startup, likelihood evaluation, and comparison to Sclove
themes.need: Someone wanting to initialize and estimate the filter's parameters needs the filter-startup procedure, the resulting sample-likelihood evaluation used for maximum-likelihood estimation, and the comparison to Sclove's (1983) alternative joint-likelihood approach.

themes.label: Smoothing: lag smoother and full-sample smoother
themes.need: Someone wanting the best possible, full-sample rather than real-time, estimate of the historical regime path needs the lag-smoother and full-sample smoother algorithms that revise the filtered probabilities using future as well as past observations.

themes.label: MLE parameter estimates for U.S. real GNP
themes.need: Someone wanting the empirical Markov-switching-model fit to postwar U.S. real GNP needs Table I's maximum-likelihood parameter estimates and the brief comparison between the four-lag and full-sample smoothed probability estimates.
themes.distributed_justification: b012-b013 form one continuous empirical-estimation narrative; the gap at 606-611 is Pass-A trash (table caption/notes), not a thematic break.

themes.label: Business-cycle dating versus NBER
themes.need: Someone wanting to compare the model's regime-based recession dating to the official NBER business-cycle chronology needs Table II's estimated recession dates and durations and their comparison to NBER dates.

themes.label: Linear vs. nonlinear model diagnostics
themes.need: Someone wanting evidence that the nonlinear Markov-switching model genuinely improves on a linear ARIMA benchmark needs the diagnostic comparison - residual autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity tests - between the two model classes fit to GNP growth.

themes.label: Prior estimates of the permanent GNP effect
themes.need: Someone wanting to situate this paper's estimate of a recession's permanent output effect against the existing literature needs Table III's summary of prior studies' estimates of the permanent effect of business-cycle fluctuations on the level of GNP.

themes.label: Business-cycle persistence and the permanent effect of a recession
themes.need: Someone wanting to quantify how much of a recession's output loss is permanent versus temporary needs the derivation and estimate of the long-run permanent effect (eq. 5.1) of a regime-switch-defined recession on the level of GNP.

themes.label: Implications for the permanent income hypothesis
themes.need: Someone wanting to connect the estimated permanent GNP effect of recessions to consumption theory needs the implications for the permanent income hypothesis (eq. 8.1-8.3), showing how a permanent recession-driven output shock should affect consumption behavior.

themes.label: Conclusions
themes.need: Someone wanting a compact summary of the paper's contribution needs the concluding characterization of recurrent regime shifts as the statistical definition of the business cycle.
